content.thinking:
This intervention counters the "models can't predict" skepticism by appealing to scientific track record, which is evidence-based and counter-attitudinal but fairly dry and technical. It mainly targets the competence subscale of trust, likely with some spillover to integrity, so I'd estimate moderate overall gains—competence up 3-4 points, other subscales up around 1-1.5, averaging roughly +2.0.

I'm now assigning specific values across the outcome measures: trust_post +1.4, distrust_post -1.1, funding_perceptions +0.8, policy_role_mean +1.0, inst_trust_mean +0.7, belief_post +1.2, concern_mean +0.9, policy_general +0.7, policy_specific_mean +0.5, behavior_mean +0.35, donation_ams +0.07 (slightly boosted since AMS ties directly to model accuracy), and newsletter_signup +0.008.

content.text: {"reasoning_summary": "The 'model accuracy' arm is a source-credibility/track-record correction: it explicitly names a common skeptic criticism ('models can't predict the future') and rebuts it with concrete, verifiable evidence (17 forecasts 1970–2001, 0.9 °C observed warming, Montreal Protocol explanation for apparent misses). Its most proximal target is the competence dimension of trust, with secondary spillover to integrity/openness because it concedes imperfection ('models are not perfect'), a candid framing that tends to enhance perceived honesty. It is counter-attitudinal evidence for the initially skeptical, which the digest suggests yields above-average trust movement, but it is fairly dry, technical and non-narrative, and it makes no claim about scientists' motives, funding, or policy — so I place it modestly above the mid-range of the 16 arms on multidimensional trust (~+2 points, d≈0.09) rather than at the top. The re-asked single items (trust_post, belief_post) are shrunk relative to the fresh battery due to within-survey anchoring, and distrust is given a smaller-magnitude negative effect since distrust items are stickier. parsed_output.reasoning_summary: The 'model accuracy' arm is a source-credibility/track-record correction: it explicitly names a common skeptic criticism ('models can't predict the future') and rebuts it with concrete, verifiable evidence (17 forecasts 1970–2001, 0.9 °C observed warming, Montreal Protocol explanation for apparent misses). Its most proximal target is the competence dimension of trust, with secondary spillover to integrity/openness because it concedes imperfection ('models are not perfect'), a candid framing that tends to enhance perceived honesty. It is counter-attitudinal evidence for the initially skeptical, which the digest suggests yields above-average trust movement, but it is fairly dry, technical and non-narrative, and it makes no claim about scientists' motives, funding, or policy — so I place it modestly above the mid-range of the 16 arms on multidimensional trust (~+2 points, d≈0.09) rather than at the top. The re-asked single items (trust_post, belief_post) are shrunk relative to the fresh battery due to within-survey anchoring, and distrust is given a smaller-magnitude negative effect since distrust items are stickier. Downstream outcomes are ordered trust > scientist role/funding attitudes > belief/concern > general/specific policy > behavioral intentions, with incentivized outcomes at a few cents and under one percentage point; the AMS donation gets a marginally larger nudge than average because a meteorological society is topically congruent with forecasting accuracy.
